I picked **candidate 5** by estimating in my head, without running a simulation.

**Order frequency.** Each order costs 34 on top of the goods, and goods sit in the warehouse for part of the cycle, which costs storage.
- **Daily orders (candidate 3)** cost about 884 in order fees. Ordering every other day saves about 442 in fees but only adds about 300 in storage.
- **Every 3 or 4 days (candidates 0, 4, 7)** saves 136 or more in order fees compared with every other day. But it adds about 300 in storage, and deliveries of 200–233 units come close to the 236-unit limit, so some may be lost.
- **Every other day** comes out best.

**Order size.** Candidates 1, 2, 5 and 6 all order every other day and differ only in how much more than the forecast they order:

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | ×1.0 | ×1.0 |
| 1 | ×1.1 | ×1.1 |
| 5 | ≈×1.05 | ≈×1.2 |
| 2 | ×1.2 | ×1.2 |

- **Product 0:** a missing unit costs 11 (7 lost margin plus a 4 penalty), and an extra unit costs about 6 plus storage. That points to ordering a bit above forecast.
- **Product 1:** a missing unit costs 14 (9 plus a 5 penalty), and an extra unit costs about 5. That points to ordering clearly above forecast.
- **Leftovers:** unsold stock keeps for 5 days, so it carries into the next delivery. That makes over-ordering cheaper.
- **Real demand:** it averages about 4.6% above forecast. Candidate 6, which orders exactly the forecast, will run short.

Candidate 5 orders a little extra of product 0 and a lot extra of product 1, which best fits these costs.

I picked **candidate 2**, based on a mental estimate, not a simulation.

1. **Shortages cost much more than surplus.** A missed unit costs its margin plus the penalty: 7 + 4 = 11 for product 0 and 9 + 5 = 14 for product 1. A surplus unit mostly carries over. Stock sells oldest first and lasts 5 days, so a leftover from a 2-day order still gets sold, at only 0.3–0.5 per day in storage. It is written off (losing the 6 or 5 paid for it) only if it stays unsold for several days running. So it pays to order well above the forecast.
2. **The mean multiplier is about 1.046.** Ordering exactly to forecast (candidates 6 and 7) is short on average, so the ×1.0 and ×1.05 plans run out more often.
3. **Ordering every 2 days versus every 3 days.** Ordering every 2 days costs 13 × 34 = 442 in daily fees, versus 9 × 34 = 306 for every 3 days, a difference of 136. Candidate 4 uses only a ×1.1 margin, and around day 19 its order of 221 units plus leftovers could exceed the 236 limit and lose some of the delivery. Candidate 0 has the same overflow risk, only worse.
4. **Candidates 2 and 5 are the same except for product 0.** Candidate 2 orders ×1.2 for both products; candidate 5 uses ×1.05 for product 0. Because a shortage of product 0 costs 11 against roughly 0.6 for storing a spare unit, the larger order (candidate 2) should come out ahead. The authors' own profit claims weren't used, since they can't be checked.

The first three days are short of stock in every plan, so they don't affect the comparison.

Я выбираю кандидата 1. Это приблизительная оценка в уме, без расчёта: он лучше остальных с умеренной, но не полной уверенностью.

**Что одинаково у всех.** Первые заказы приходят только на 4-й день. До этого спрос на дни 0–3 (около 99 и 144 единиц) превышает стартовый запас (40 и 48), так что все планы одинаково платят неустойку за эти дни. Различает их частота заказов и запас сверх прогноза.

**Частота заказов.** Это баланс между платой 34 за день заказа и хранением запаса между приходами (в среднем около 0,4 за единицу в день).
- **Каждый день (кандидат 3):** 26 платежей, около 884. По сравнению с заказом раз в 2 дня это примерно на 440 дороже, а хранения экономится только около 300. Кроме того, запаса около 10 % мало, если спрос за один день колеблется примерно на 30 %.
- **Раз в 2 дня (кандидаты 1, 2, 5, 6):** 13 платежей, около 442; между приходами на складе в среднем около 30 единиц.
- **Раз в 3 дня (кандидаты 4, 7):** платежей на 4 меньше, экономия около 136. Но среднего запаса на складе примерно на 30 единиц больше, это около 300 лишнего хранения.
- **Раз в 4 дня (кандидат 0):** хранение дороже ещё примерно на 600, а экономия на платежах около 200. Заказ ровно по прогнозу, без запаса. Партии почти заполняют склад (233 из 236), поэтому остаток прошлой партии может вытеснить часть новой при приходе.

Значит, лучшая частота — раз в 2 дня.

**Сколько заказывать сверх прогноза.** Нехватка обходится в 11–14 за единицу (потерянная маржа плюс неустойка), лишняя единица — в 5–6 плюс хранение. Средний множитель спроса около 1,046, поэтому заказ ровно по прогнозу в среднем систематически даёт нехватку. Остатки при этом не пропадают сразу: при годности 5 дней они почти всегда продаются в следующем цикле. Поэтому перебор с запасом превращается в растущий запас, за который платится хранение, а то, что останется к концу, ничего не стоит.
- **Кандидат 6 (×1,0):** нехватка примерно 6–7 единиц каждого товара за цикл, около 80 единиц за весь срок по каждому. Это примерно на 200 хуже кандидата 1.
- **Кандидат 1 (около ×1,1):** запас растёт медленно, около 3 единиц за цикл, и нехватка заметно снижается. По моей оценке, это наилучший баланс.
- **Кандидат 2 (около ×1,2):** запас растёт примерно на 9 единиц за цикл. Он докупает около 72 единиц товара 0, из них продаётся лишь около четверти, и хранение выходит примерно на 230 дороже. По товару 0 он хуже кандидата 1 примерно на 300, по товару 1 картина похожая.
- **Кандидат 5:** товара 0 заказывает почти ровно по среднему спросу (×1,05), товара 1 — с избытком (×1,2). По обоим товарам он немного хуже кандидата 1.

Разрыв между кандидатами 1, 2 и 5 невелик — по моей прикидке несколько сотен, — поэтому уверенность умеренная, но достаточная, чтобы не отказываться от выбора.

I chose **candidate 1**: on these estimates it should give the highest expected profit. I worked this out by reasoning only, with no step-by-step simulation, so the numbers below are rough.

**How often to order.** Each order costs 34 on top of the goods.
- **Every 2 days** (candidates 1, 2, 5, 6) costs 13 × 34 = 442 in order fees. This is the best trade-off.
- **Every day** (candidate 3) costs 884, about 440 more. It saves only about 300 in storage.
- **Every 3 days** (candidates 4, 7) saves 136 in order fees. But it adds roughly 0.5 day of demand to average stock, about 12 per day or around 300 over the month.
- **Every 4 days** (candidate 0) means deliveries of about 230 units, close to the 236 capacity. Any leftover stock pushes the total over the limit, and the excess is lost. It also has the highest storage cost.

**How much to order.** The every-2-day candidates differ in how far they order above the forecast for each 2-day window. Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast, which is about 63 units per window. Day-to-day variation over a window is about 13 units. Unsold stock carries over to the next window, so what matters is the steady drift between orders and demand. These are rough per-window costs for good 0:
- **Candidate 6** orders at the forecast (×1.0). The drift is about −3 units a window, so there are shortages of about 3 units each time, at a penalty of 11–14 per unit. Total about 49.
- **Candidate 1** orders at ×1.1. The drift is about +3. About 3.4 units expire, there are almost no shortages (about 0.4 units) and stock costs some storage. Total about 44.
- **Candidate 2** orders at ×1.2. The drift is about +9. About 9 units expire every window at 5–6 per unit, and the extra stock costs more storage. Total about 84, and good 1 is about as bad.
- **Candidate 5** orders good 0 at about the forecast, which is close to candidate 1 (about 41). But it orders good 1 at ×1.2. For good 1 that costs about 95 per window, against about 55 for candidate 1.

Candidate 1 is also the most robust. Missing a sale costs 11–14 per unit and expiry only 5–6, so a moderate buffer absorbs random swings without much spoilage.

I'd pick **candidate 4**. This is a mental estimate, not a simulation, and it's a close call against candidate 1.

1. **How often each plan orders.** Ordering every 3 days (candidates 4 and 7) means about 9 order days instead of 13 for the every-2-days plans (1, 2, 5, 6). That saves about 4 × 34 = 136 in fixed fees. Daily ordering (candidate 3) costs about 26 × 34 = 884 in fees, so it loses. Ordering every 4 days (candidate 0) brings about 233 units per delivery, against a 236-unit warehouse limit. Any leftover stock would push it over, and the overflow would be lost.

2. **How much each plan orders against expected demand.** On average, actual demand is about 1.05 × the forecast. Running short costs about 17 per unit: 13 − 6 = 7 in lost profit plus a penalty of about 4–5. Ordering too much is cheaper because unsold units roll over to the next days and only spoil after 5 days. So ordering a bit more than expected demand pays off.
   - Candidate 7 orders about 1.0 × forecast. That is below expected demand, so it will run short more often.
   - Candidate 4 orders about 1.1 × forecast, slightly above expected demand. Over 3 days the random swings partly cancel out (spread about ±17% instead of about ±21% over 2 days), so 1.1× covers demand fairly reliably.
   - Among the every-2-days plans, 1.0× (candidate 6) runs short too often. 1.2× (candidates 2 and 5) piles up stock, and the extra eventually spoils.

3. **Remaining risk for candidate 4.** On some days, such as day 19 (an arrival of 221 units plus leftovers), it may go slightly over the 236 limit. The fee savings and the steadier coverage should still outweigh that.

I estimated this by reasoning only, without simulating any plan. My pick is **candidate 1**, but candidate 2 is very close and could come out ahead.

1. **How often to order.** Ordering every 2 days fits the 5-day shelf life and costs 13 × 34 = 442 in fixed fees. Daily ordering (candidate 3) costs 26 × 34 = 884 in fees. Its quantities also look shifted against the 4-day lead time: for example, the day-0 order matches the forecast for day 2, but it arrives on day 4. Large orders every 3–4 days (candidates 0, 4, 7) leave stock on the shelf longer, so they pay more for storage and lose more to spoilage. That leaves candidates 1, 2, 5 and 6.

2. **How much to order.** These four differ only in how far each order exceeds the forecast for the two days it covers. Taking the first order, which covers days 4–5:
   - Candidate 6: about 1.0× forecast for both products.
   - Candidate 1: about 1.1× for both.
   - Candidate 2: about 1.2× for both.
   - Candidate 5: about 1.05× for product 0 and 1.2× for product 1.

3. **Trade-off.** A missing unit costs the lost margin plus the penalty: 11 for product 0 and 14 for product 1. An extra unit costs at most its purchase price plus storage, and usually less, because leftovers sell first in the next delivery window. On average demand is about 1.046× the forecast, so 1.0× (candidate 6) runs short too often. For product 0, 1.05× (candidate 5) gives almost no safety margin. Without carryover the best levels would be about 1.13× for product 0 and 1.19× for product 1. Carryover lowers the safety stock you need, and anything still on the shelf at the end is worthless. That puts the best level near 1.1×, so candidate 1 wins over candidate 2.

I picked **candidate 2**. This is a mental estimate, not a simulation, and the choice between candidates 2, 5 and 1 is close.

1. **Days 0–3 are the same for everyone.** No order can arrive before day 4, so all plans get through the first four days on the starting stock alone.

2. **Order frequency.** Each order costs a fixed 34. Holding one day's demand of both goods costs about 0.3·30 + 0.5·30 ≈ 24 per day.
   - **Every 2 days** (candidates 1, 2, 5, 6): 13 orders, 442 in fixed costs. Average leftover stock is about half a day's demand, so holding is about 12 per day.
   - **Every 3 days** (candidates 4, 7): 4 fewer orders saves 136. But leftover stock doubles, adding about 12 × 26 ≈ 312 in holding, so it loses overall.
   - **Daily** (candidate 3): about 312 less holding, but 442 more in fixed costs. It also loses.
   - **Every 4 days** (candidate 0): even more stock and it runs into the 236-unit warehouse limit. It is the worst.

3. **Order size among the every-2-days plans.** These plans order the forecast for the next two days times a factor: candidate 6 uses 1.0, candidate 1 uses 1.1, candidate 5 uses 1.05 for good 0 and 1.2 for good 1, and candidate 2 uses 1.2 for both.
   - Running short of good 0 costs about 13 − 6 + 4 = 11 per unit. Running short of good 1 costs about 9 + 5 = 14.
   - Over-ordering costs at most the purchase price (6 or 5), plus storage. Leftovers carry over and sell first in the next cycle, so the full price is only lost if a unit spoils.
   - Demand averages about 1.046 × forecast, and a two-day total varies by roughly ±21%. Balancing those costs gives an ideal factor of about 1.13 for good 0 and about 1.19 for good 1.
   - Because leftovers carry over, it's better to lean high. That points to candidate 2 (1.2 for both) over candidate 5 (1.05 / 1.2) and candidate 1 (1.1).

I picked **candidate 1** from a rough mental estimate, without simulating any plan. Candidate 5 comes very close, so this is a judgement call.

1. **Order every 2 days.** Ordering daily (candidate 3) means 26 order fees of 34, which costs too much. Ordering every 3 or 4 days roughly doubles the stock held between deliveries. The extra holding cost, about 12 per day, is more than the 136 saved on fees. Large deliveries also risk going over the 236-unit limit. Candidate 0's first delivery of 233 units arrives on top of leftover stock, so it will overflow. Candidate 4 delivers 221 units on day 19 and may overflow too.
2. **Order a modest buffer above forecast.** True demand averages about 1.046 × forecast. For each product, I weighed the cost of running short against the cost of an extra unit that spoils:
   - Product 0: a short unit costs about 11 (7 lost margin + 4 penalty), and a spoiled unit about 7.5. That gives about 0.6, so the order should be roughly 1.08–1.10 × forecast.
   - Product 1: a short unit costs about 14 (9 + 5), and a spoiled unit about 6.5. That gives about 0.65–0.7. Leftovers can still be sold in the next 2-day window, which lowers the best buffer to about +7 units per order, or roughly 1.1–1.15 × forecast.
3. **Compare the 2-day plans:**
   - Candidate 6 (exactly the forecast) will run short too often.
   - Candidate 2 (×1.2 on both) builds up a steady surplus that spoils.
   - Candidate 1 (×1.1 on both) is close to the best level for product 0 and slightly low for product 1.
   - Candidate 5 (×1.05 on product 0, ×1.2 on product 1) is low on product 0 and high on product 1.

Since leftovers carry into the next window, slightly lower orders tend to win, so I chose candidate 1.

I chose **Candidate 2** (orders every 2 days, 1.2× the forecast for both products). I estimated this in my head without simulating, so the margins below are rough.

- **Running short costs more than over-ordering.** A missing unit of product 0 loses its 7 margin plus a 4 penalty, 11 in total. Product 1 loses 9 plus 5, 14 in total. An extra unit only risks its purchase price (6 or 5) plus storage, so it pays to order above expected demand.
- **Expected demand is already above forecast.** The average multiplier is about 1.046. Ordering exactly to forecast (Candidates 6 and 7) or at 1.05× for product 0 (Candidate 5) will often run short.
- **Leftovers aren't wasted right away.** Each batch lasts 5 days, but a 2-day cycle only needs about 2 days of stock. Surplus carries into the next cycle and is written off only if it sits too long. That makes a 1.2× buffer cheap.
- **Ordering every 2 days is the best trade-off.** Each order day costs a fixed 34. Ordering daily (Candidate 3) pays it 26 times, which is too often. The 3- and 4-day plans (Candidates 4, 7 and 0) hold more stock and have bigger forecast errors per batch. Candidate 0 also runs close to the 236-unit capacity.
- **Days 0–3 don't decide it.** No order arrives before day 4, so every plan has the same shortages over that stretch.

The authors' own claimed results weren't used to make the choice.

I'd pick **Candidate 1**: ordering every 2 days at 1.1× the forecast. I worked this out by hand with a rough newsvendor estimate and no simulation, and the leaders are close, so treat it as a judgement call.

- **How often to order:** Every plan is stuck with the same shortages on days 0–3, because the starting stock is 40 and 48 units and nothing can arrive before day 4. Ordering every 2 days fits well. Each batch is about 130 units, well under the 236 capacity, and items last 5 days, so leftovers can still sell in the next cycle. Ordering daily (Candidate 3) costs about 26 order fees of 34 each. Ordering every 3–4 days (Candidates 0, 4, 7) means bigger batches, more storage cost and getting close to the capacity limit.
- **How much for product 0:** A missing unit costs 11 (7 lost margin plus 4 penalty), and an unsold unit costs about 6. That puts the best order a little above average demand. Since actual demand averages about 1.046× the forecast, 1.1× the forecast is only about 5% over the average. That came out cheapest: about 1.35 per unit of demand, versus about 1.45 at 1.05× and about 1.44 at 1.2×.
- **How much for product 1:** A shortage costs more (14), so 1.2× the forecast is slightly better here. That's why Candidate 5 (1.05× for product 0, 1.2× for product 1) is close behind. But its product 0 orders only match average demand, and that loss is a bit larger than its gain on product 1. Storage for product 1 (0.5 per unit per day) also works against keeping extra stock.
- **Other candidates:** Candidate 2 (1.2× on both) adds about 15% surplus every cycle, and with a fixed plan much of it eventually spoils. Candidate 6 (exactly the forecast) runs short too often.

I estimated this roughly in my head without running a simulation, so the pick is a judgement call. **I'd choose candidate 1.** I'm fairly confident a 2-day plan is best, but the gap between candidates 1 and 5 is small.

**What the candidates are.** Each plan scales the forecast for the days it covers:
- **Every 2 days:** candidates 6, 1, 2 and 5 order the forecast for the next two days multiplied by 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, and 1.05 for product 0 with 1.2 for product 1.
- **Every 3 days:** candidates 7 and 4 use multipliers of 1.0 and 1.1.
- **Every 4 days:** candidate 0 uses 1.0.
- **Daily:** candidate 3 orders 1.1 times the next day's forecast.

**How often to order.**
- **Daily (candidate 3):** 26 orders cost 884 in fixed fees, compared with 442 for 13 orders every 2 days. More frequent ordering doesn't win back that difference.
- **Every 3 days (candidates 4 and 7):** they save 136 in fees. But they hold about 30 more units each day at 0.3–0.5 per unit, which costs roughly 300. They lose overall.
- **Every 4 days (candidate 0):** each delivery is about 233 units, which nearly fills the 236-unit warehouse. Any leftover stock means part of the delivery is lost on arrival, and holding costs are higher.

**How much safety stock to order every 2 days.** Leftovers carry into the next cycle, because goods last 5 days and a new batch arrives every 2.
- **1.2:** this is well above the average demand multiplier of 1.046. Stock keeps building until it spoils. That wastes about 15% of purchases, roughly 120 units of each product, or about 600–740 in purchase cost plus holding.
- **1.0:** stock just follows random demand, and shortages cost 11–14 per unit.
- **About 1.1:** stock grows slightly, which covers random dips without much spoilage. This is the most balanced choice.

Candidate 1 uses 1.1 for both products, so it comes out ahead. Candidate 5 (1.05 for product 0, 1.2 for product 1) is the close runner-up.

I picked **candidate 1**, based on reasoning rather than a calculation. I didn't simulate any plan, and the authors' claimed totals weren't checked.

1. **Order every 2 days.** That means 13 fixed payments of 34 (442 total). Ordering daily (candidate 3) means 26 payments (884), and the 3-day plans don't save enough to outweigh it. Two days of demand fits well inside the 5-day shelf life, so leftovers can still be sold in the next period.
2. **Leftovers carry over and sell first.** Unsold stock is used before the next batch, so a small surplus in each order builds a safety buffer. Stock is only written off when the leftover exceeds the next period's demand.
3. **Size orders slightly above mean demand.** Demand averages about 1.046 × the forecast, so ordering exactly the forecast (candidate 6, ×1.0) or ×1.05 for product 0 (candidate 5) leaves almost no surplus to build a buffer, and shortages become frequent. Ordering ×1.2 (candidate 2) builds a buffer quickly, but the extra roughly 15% of each order mostly expires (costing 5–6 per unit) while preventing few extra shortages.
4. **×1.1 on both products is the middle ground.** The buffer forms, and only about 5% excess per period is written off.
5. **Candidate 0 can overflow the warehouse.** It orders 4 days of demand at once, about 230 units of both products together. That's close to the 236-unit capacity before counting any leftovers, so some of each delivery could be lost on arrival.

I chose **Candidate 2**, based on rough mental estimates. I didn't simulate any plan exactly.

1. **Order every 2 days.**
   - Every-2-day plans place 13 orders and pay 442 in fixed fees.
   - Daily ordering (Candidate 3) adds 442 in fees but saves only about 300 in holding.
   - Every 3 days (Candidates 4 and 7) saves 136 in fees but adds about 300 in holding.
   - Every 4 days (Candidate 0) saves about 238 in fees but adds about 600 in holding. Its batches of up to 233 units also nearly fill the 236-unit warehouse, leaving no room for a buffer.
2. **Size each order at about 1.2 × forecast for both products.** Candidates 1, 2, 5 and 6 differ only in this multiplier.
   - Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast.
   - Running short costs more than overstocking. For product 0 a missing unit costs 11 (7 lost margin + 4 penalty) and a spare one about 6. That points to about the 65th percentile of demand, or about 1.13 × forecast.
   - For product 1 the costs are 14 and about 5. That points to about the 74th percentile, or about 1.19 × forecast.
   - Spare stock keeps for 5 days, so leftovers usually sell in the next cycle. That makes overstocking cheaper still and pushes both products toward 1.2.
3. **Candidate 2 is the only plan at about 1.2 for both products.** Candidates 6 and 1 are at 1.0 and 1.1. Candidate 5 uses 1.2 only for product 1 and 1.05 for product 0. On the first 4 days every plan runs short equally, because nothing ordered can arrive before day 4.

**Выбираю кандидата 1.** Уверенность умеренная: он лучший по расчёту, но 2 и 5 отстают от него ненамного. Всё посчитано в уме, без моделирования.

**Что общее у всех.** Первые заказы приходят только на день 4. Стартового запаса (40 и 48 единиц) хватает примерно на 1–2 дня, поэтому в днях 1–3 нехватка с неустойкой будет у всех кандидатов. Разница между планами начинается с дня 4.

**Как часто заказывать.** Сравниваю, сколько стоят дни с заказом (по 34) и сколько стоит хранение, если партии крупнее. При спросе около 30 единиц в день по каждому товару и хранении 0.3 + 0.5:
- **Каждый день (кандидат 3):** 26 дней с заказом, это 884. Платить приходится на 442 больше, чем при заказе раз в 2 дня, а хранение экономит только около 310.
- **Раз в 2 дня (кандидаты 1, 2, 5, 6):** 13 дней с заказом, это 442. Самый выгодный вариант.
- **Раз в 3 дня (кандидаты 4, 7):** экономия на заказах 136, но средний вечерний остаток больше примерно на 15 единиц каждого товара. Хранение дороже примерно на 310.
- **Раз в 4 дня (кандидат 0):** хранение дороже примерно на 620. Кроме того, партия около 233 единиц почти заполняет склад на 236. Утром дня прихода на складе ещё лежит остаток прошлой партии (она списывается только вечером), так что излишек пропадает. При этом запаса сверх среднего спроса почти нет.

**Сколько заказывать.** Средний множитель спроса 1,046. Потеря от нехватки за единицу: товар 0 — 7 + 4 = 11, товар 1 — 9 + 5 = 14. Потеря от излишка — закупка (6 и 5) плюс хранение. Остаток партии ещё продаётся в следующем цикле, потому что годность 5 дней, а новая партия приходит через 2. С учётом этого выгодно заказывать примерно в 1,10–1,12 раза больше среднего для товара 0 и примерно в 1,15 раза для товара 1.

Насколько больше среднего спроса заказывают кандидаты с заказом раз в 2 дня:

| Кандидат | Товар 0 | Товар 1 | Оценка |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ×1,10 | ×1,10 | ближе всех к выгодному объёму |
| 2 | ×1,20 | ×1,20 | лишнее списывается |
| 5 | ×1,05 | ×1,20 | товара 0 мало, товара 1 много |
| 6 | ×1,00 | ×1,00 | частые нехватки |

У кандидата 1 есть запас на случай, если спрос окажется выше прогноза. При этом он не переплачивает за списание, как кандидат 2, а склад не переполняется.

**Выбор: кандидат 2.** Расчёт приблизительный, в уме, по средним значениям; разница между тремя лучшими планами с заказом раз в 2 дня (2, 5, 1) небольшая.

**Что одинаково у всех.** Ни один заказ не приходит раньше дня 4. Поэтому нехватка в дни 0–3 у всех планов одна и та же и на выбор не влияет. Главные различия в трёх вещах: плата 34 за каждый день заказа, хранение (оно растёт с размером партии) и уровень заказа относительно ожидаемого спроса.

**Частота заказов: выигрывает раз в 2 дня.**
